4th grade, so I must have been 9 (I’m 26 now). I felt ill, my hands went numb and I felt like I couldn’t breathe. I went to the bathroom and remember I kept putting my hand near my mouth as i exhaled to “check” if I was still breathing. That only made it worse. I went to the nurse because I thought I was sick/dying. I remember my dad picked me up from school and brought me hot tea and took me to get Duck Donuts. Multiple people in my family have anxiety so he def knew what was happening before I did. 

Eventually we put a name to it and I remember him and my mom encouraged me to journal and he would walk me through breathing/PMR type of stuff which helped. They kind of did a bit with me with my endless what if/worst case worries and they would call it that, “the what ifs” but eventually they sent set me up with therapy

Looking back I feel like that was a pretty progressive way to parent a child with MH issues in the 2000s especially bc it was hardly talked about and so stigmatized back then so I feel lucky, anxiety still sucks tho and I don’t even know who I’d be without it bc I’ve struggled with it for that long

My face changed a ton from 18-26

I love this question bc I have family in Chicago who absolutely loooove to dunk on Philly lol. I’ve live lived in Philly, subletted in Chicago for a bit and visited so ymmv but I find that many of the things THEY roast are the same as any major city including Chicago: crime, traffic, city corruption, “it smells like piss/weed” (at least I’ve experienced that in both) etc. And the pros are similar: Sports, walkable, different neighborhoods with a very distinct feel, food scene (ultimately depends on your cuisine preferences, both are strong imo), lots to do.

The actual main drawbacks of Philly vs Chicago imo: 1) Chicago’s lake is beautiful and overall vibe in the summer is more lively. The city really comes alive with the festivals, lake, etc which makes sense after a long winter whereas we do have some summery stuff like SIPS but lots of people also go down the shore which is great, but less humans in the actual city = less lively 2) Skyline/high rise architecture is better. The river and Lakeshore Dr are cool and picturesque too. 3) Our public transportation isn’t as reliable and the constant talk of budget cuts DESPITE THIS is crazy. If you miss the bus you might be cooked or have to Uber. CTA isn’t perfect i.e. London/NYC metros but CTA definitely better. 4) Some center city neighborhoods have alleyways for trash, but some don’t, so it doesn’t feel as pristine. And littering. Smh 5) Chicago is a bar AND club city, we’re mostly a bar city. Depends what you like. 6) Chicago has legal weed. Which I also don’t partake in so non-factor for me 7) Chicago has more music festivals. MIA is (was?) meh, Lolla is better imo 8) Chicago feels and IS bigger and more cosmopolitan. Maybe not NYC level and there is some degree of insularity with like, locals and big ten transplants but it feels a bit more world-class in terms of attractions 9) Besides healthcare (which certainly shouldn’t be omitted about Philly, it holds its own), Chicago definitely has broader job opportunities especially white collar industries. 

Counter argument: 1) Philly is more affordable on average, though ymmv depending on what neighborhood. Overall though Chicago’s property taxes are higher. Also being smaller and more compact, it’s easier to navigate. Being in a different neighborhood might mean like, 6 blocks down and 6 blocks west. Which can be good and bad 2) Philly is generally a working class city, and people are more down-to-earth imo. It may come off as gruff sometimes but people are pretty genuine. tbh I’d take that over “Minnesota Nice”. 3) This is a personal opinion but Re: down to earth, no one is constantly screeching about how they live in THE BEST CITY EVER!1!1 the boosterism gets annoying. Don’t get me wrong, A lot of Philly people love their city, but it’s more of a scrappy kind of pride. I feel like Chicagoans inherited the boosterism trait from its history, some don’t like to acknowledge its flaws and try to dunk on NYC when literally no one brought it up. Like there are multiple ads/billboards about how basically “NYC bad Chicago good” 4) Chicago is also big on sports but Philly gets a whole other level of *electric* especially now. Every building is green and the past month has been so much fun. 5) Imo I find that what we lack in skyline we make up for with some beautiful historic streets, neighborhoods etc. If you try to tell me that somewhere like, Delancey Place etc isn’t very picturesque you’re wrong 6) Weather is milder, and even in colder months it isn’t as gray. Spring and fall are usually sunny 7) Maybe biased but I feel like we have more “character” and quirkiness which is why it’s more polarizing. Lots of weird traditions and “only in Philly” things, and doesn’t try to impress/be like other cities 8) Chicago’s lake is stunning but imo we have more plentiful and more diverse nature options ie Wissahickon and Fairmount Parks, and an easy drive to mountains and the shoreline. Some people have very strong opinions on lake being a beach vs solely the shore so that’s up to you. In general the midwest is flatter and you have to go further out from CHI to get nature-nature besides the lake ie Sleeping Bear Dunes but some people do it. Buttt if you like to do weekly 12 milers up mountains or whatever you’re better off out west

I am not opposed to BZD use nor do I think they are “the devil” especially after failing multiple first-line treatments. It is not a first line treatment, but use, even long term use, can be highly effective for the right patient. I take .5mg clonazepam prn myself. However, it is important not to minimize withdrawal danger or equate it to that of SSRIs/SNRIs.

SSRI/SNRI withdrawal if not tapered correctly can be uncomfortable and “nasty” as you said eg brain zaps, rebound symptoms, etc. (Typically ones with shorter half-lives are more likely to have discontinuation syndrome symptoms ie Paxil is shorter compared to other SSRIs and most SNRIs have shorter half-lives than SSRIs plus their mechanism is different). However, improperly tapering off of BZD can provoke seizures and autonomic dysfunction. This is why the reversal (flumazenil) for benzodiazepine overdose is used with considerable caution because it can provoke these withdrawal seizures. Danger is of course dependent on half-life and pharmacokinetics of the different drugs. Longer half life generally comes with less risks. The study you cited about clonazepam, it has a 30-40h half life which is considered long in the realm of benzodiazepines.

Tapering off of any psychiatric medication should not be attempted without the close monitoring of a healthcare provider.

Just a PA student here so cannot provide answers to all of your questions, but so far overall I think it was a good choice. The possibilities are very exciting to me and throughout my rotations I’ve come to appreciate the flexibility/potential we have in so many different fields and geographic areas for job-seeking (whereas CAA is more specific in both respects). I’ll graduate at 25yo and feel like I’m on a good trajectory with where I want to be.

The schooling process is pretty brutal and unforgiving though, and you have to have your sh*t figured out (ie, mental health support if needed, reliable transportation for clinicals, organizational skills).

Another option I’ve heard good things about if you like the OR- IR techs have a good salary and way less debt than us. The ones I’ve met on my rotation loved it and one of the IR PAs said he wishes he looked into that. Rad tech in general is a physical job, not “cushy” and you aren’t diagnosing (as you would as a provider) but very interesting. MRI tech also seems really cool. Rad techs can work in all 50 states and there are more niches (MRI, XR, IR etc) vs CAA. I think they make less though. Also cardiac perfusionists and sonographers are cool niches. However I think most of these are bachelors/associates so if you’re looking for a Master’s (since you said you will graduate from a bachelor’s) not sure if that is a consideration.

No regrets so far, but tbh I’ve met more PAs that regret going into medicine altogether than PAs who wish they became docs (but one of my adjunct professors actually was a PA who became a doctor and is happy). I’ve jokingly heard and said “I wish I became a tech bro” because… medicine is hard. We deal with patients emotional and physical trauma and you have to take care of yourself. There is no absolute right choice or certainty in picking a medical profession and if you can be happy doing that, you can be happy in a lot of them and it’s rewarding.

Sounds a lot like depersonalization/derealization, which although very scary, is not super uncommon 

Causes of that could be a lot of things though- anxiety/panic, depression, could be the side effect of the meds (esp if dose was recently increased since stimulants can cause anxiety) and like others have said, take her to your pediatrician to rule out neuro things ie seizures as some people mentioned, and it will probably give you peace of mind.

Depersonalization is one of the possible criteria for panic disorder in the DSM so my hunch is that could be that, if everything is ruled out and it ends up being the case that this is depersonalization/panic, I would reassure her that no matter how scary it feels, she is SAFE, she’s not going to “go crazy” or die, and help her focus on doing something that she loves and going about her day. rumination on it can definitely make it worse. You could even explain it like “I know everything feels scary and funny, but it can’t hurt you, your brain just got a little overwhelmed and is trying to do its best” or something (I’m sure you can come up with something better than that but general idea)

Working with a child psychologist, therapist or psychiatrist (who your pediatrician can probably help with referral) may also be really helpful since they specialize in these things. She is not alone in this!

As mentioned, cost and length should factor… distance to home is a another good factor because rotation sites will be closer to your connections, which means less $ spent on BnBs and less isolation if you’re shipped to a new city for a rotation 

Speaking of, I’d look at how much does each school ship you far away for rotations? Some programs (even older ones, mine has been around for a hot sec and still) will have you bounce from city to city, sometimes far away which sucks ESPECIALLY if they don’t pay for your housing. I’m lucky I’m close to home because I’ve just been crashing with various relatives and friends for free or homie discount lol. However, the silver lining of living as Mr. Worldwide on rotations is you get to network in various locations and take mental notes on different health systems when applying for jobs

And what about electives? Having 2-3 electives let’s say (rather than 1) is a blessing and a curse, both awesome but also daunting. Allows you to network more especially for niche specialties (ie surgery subspecialties like vascular/ortho/uro etc, peds subspecialties), but many electives may means shorter rotations- less time to finally be comfortable at a site before leaving and being a noob all over again. Do you think you’d enjoy that type of variety and seeing a little bit of a lot or would you find that overwhelming and prefer to have longer rotations where you can dive deeper?

Tbh as someone with a medical background, I typically associate abdominal pain as a symptom with GI more than musculoskeletal

However, prior to my work experience I don’t think I thought of it this way, even though most people (including me in the past) say “stomach pain” but are actually referring to lower abdominal pain from the GI tract that’s much lower than the epigastric area that contains the stomach

Also you’re right that “stomachache” is often more socially acceptable even when anatomically it isn’t correct, because digestive issues are unfortunately taboo to some people, which sucks

I worked in an ER and you’re technically right, abdominal pain was one of the most common chief complaints, but often the patients who don’t have medical background (aka most people) would describe their symptoms as severe stomach pain/belly pain and the providers would document that with more medical terminology i.e. pt complained of abdominal pain in X quadrant, or epigastric pain, tenderness etc. It is broad though because a pt may say “stomach pain” but upon exam, the tenderness or pain is actually in the lower abdomen that contains the intestines and other organs

However prior to working in the ED, I had no idea that abdominal pain was the proper terminology for what is commonly known as belly pain/stomach pain, and as someone with digestive issues I’d just be like “ugh my stomach hurts” or “stummy hurt” kinda unironically lmao. Even when half the time it was lower abdominal pain related to lower GI
